title: Vayeshev: wanting to settle (Genesis 37:1)
hookLine: Rashi: Jacob wished to live in peace, and Joseph's troubles sprang upon him

cards: The move is done, the boxes are unpacked, the kids are finally sleeping through the night. You sit down on the couch and think: now, finally, calm. That's usually when the phone rings.
Jacob's life has been like a storm. A brother who wanted him dead. Twenty years with a difficult uncle.
Wrestling, limping, burying his mother's nurse, and his beloved Rachel. Now he's home. This portion is called Vayeshev, and he settled.

teach.b: It opens with a quiet verse: Jacob settled in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan. Notice the two verbs. His father Isaac sojourned there, lived like a guest.
Jacob wants to settle, to sit down, to stay. The very next verse starts the story of Joseph: a seventeen-year-old, a favorite son, a coat, some dreams, and brothers who hate him.
Within a chapter, Joseph is gone and Jacob is tearing his clothes in grief. Rashi, reading those two verses side by side, drew on an old midrash.
Jacob wished to dwell in tranquility, he says, and the troubles of Joseph sprang upon him.

Then a sharp line: the righteous want to live at ease in this world too, and God says, isn't what's waiting for them in the world to come enough? That can sound harsh. But Rashi isn't mocking the wish for peace.
He's noticing a pattern in the text. One way to hear it: calm is real, but it isn't a place you move into and own.
It comes, and it goes. Hard years are still ahead of Jacob, and some of his sweetest too. In the end, he'll see Joseph again.
Vayeshev comes from the same root as yeshivah, a place where you sit and study, and as the word for sitting in a home.
Jewish life has plenty of sitting: at the Shabbat table, in study, even in mourning, when a family sits shivah, the seven days, low to the ground.
Jewish life treats rest as holy. The text just never promises it will last.

how: Vayeshev is read in synagogues in early winter, often near Hanukkah, and Rashi's comment on Jacob's wish for tranquility is taught alongside it.

o: and he sojourned, living like a guest
and he settled, Jacob sitting down at home
and he dreamed, for Joseph's dreams

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: seventeen, with a coat and dreams
he wished for calm; troubles sprang

s: the Joseph story begins right after Jacob settles
the next verse starts Joseph's story, and trouble follows within a chapter.
Rashi says wanting peace is wrong
he notices that calm, though real, isn't guaranteed in this world.
vayeshev shares a root with yeshivah
both come from the Hebrew root for sitting. shivah is a different word: it means seven.

games.q: after years of storms you're finally home. you're Jacob. what do you hope for?
games.why: Jacob wished to dwell in tranquility, Rashi says, and the troubles of Joseph sprang upon him.

practice: Notice any calm there is right now, even a little: the chair holding you, the quiet in the room, or the noise you've gotten used to, and enjoy it without clutching.
Then let yourself know it will change, and that you've come through changes before. Hold both: this rest is real, and it doesn't have to last forever to be good.

wordCard.voice: Vayeshev. And he settled: the portion where Jacob finally sits down, and the troubles of Joseph begin.

orig.note: Hebrew: and he settled, sat, dwelt. the first word of the portion.

carryVoice: Your line: rest comes and goes. For Jacob, it went within a chapter. See you soon.
